title: Git & GitHub: Commit, Branch & Pull Requests
plainExplanation: Git is a time-machine for code. It records every change you make so you can roll back bugs, experiment safely on separate branches, and merge work seamlessly. GitHub is a cloud platform where developers host Git repositories and collaborate through Pull Requests (PRs).
whyItMatters: No software engineer works in isolation. Git is the universal collaboration protocol for modern software engineering teams worldwide.
learningObjectives: Initialize repositories, stage changes with git add, and commit with meaningful messages
Create, switch, and merge git branches
Push code to remote repositories and open Pull Requests
commonMistakes: Committing API secrets or node_modules because .gitignore was missing
Force pushing (`git push -f`) to shared main branches

questions.prompt: You modified `app.py`. What command sequence saves this change to your local commit history with a descriptive message?
options: git add app.py && git commit -m 'Fix authentication bug'
questions.correctAnswer: git add app.py && git commit -m 'Fix authentication bug'
questions.explanation: `git add` stages changes to the index, and `git commit` records staged changes in the local commit history.

title: Data Structures: Arrays, Hash Maps & Complexity (Big-O)
plainExplanation: Data structures are specialized ways to organize and store data in memory so operations can be done efficiently. Big-O notation measures how memory (Space) and computation time (Time) scale as input size grows from 10 items to 10 million items.
whyItMatters: An inefficient algorithm with $O(N^2)$ complexity can freeze a server when processing 100,000 users, whereas an $O(N)$ or $O(1)$ algorithm handles it in milliseconds.
learningObjectives: Calculate Time and Space complexity using Big-O notation
Implement and use Hash Maps / Dictionaries for $O(1)$ average lookups
Differentiate between dynamic arrays, linked lists, stacks, and queues
commonMistakes: Using nested loops to search a list when a hash set or dictionary lookup takes $O(1)$ time
Assuming Big-O measures exact milliseconds rather than asymptotic scaling rate

codingChallenge.title: Two Sum Optimal Hash Map
codingChallenge.instructions: Given a list of integers `nums` and an integer `target`, return the indices of the two numbers such that they add up to `target` in $O(N)$ time. You may assume exactly one solution exists.
codingChallenge.solutionHint: Check if `target - num` is already in `seen`. If yes, return `[seen[target - num], i]`. Otherwise store `seen[num] = i`.

questions.prompt: What is the average time complexity of looking up a key in a Python dictionary / Hash Table?
questions.explanation: Hash tables compute a hash of the key to index directly into a bucket array, providing constant O(1) time on average.

title: Relational Databases, SQL & Data Modeling
plainExplanation: A relational database (like PostgreSQL or SQLite) stores structured data in tables with rows and columns, linked by foreign keys. SQL (Structured Query Language) is the standardized language to query, insert, update, and manage this data with ACID reliability.
whyItMatters: Applications require persistent, consistent data. Whether managing bank transactions or social media posts, software engineers must design clean schemas and prevent data anomalies.
learningObjectives: Design normalized database schemas with Primary and Foreign Keys
Write SQL SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, and JOIN queries
Understand indexes and query optimization principles
commonMistakes: Performing filtering in client memory instead of writing an indexed SQL WHERE clause
Neglecting Foreign Key constraints leading to orphaned database records

questions.prompt: Which SQL JOIN returns all rows from the left table, and the matched rows from the right table (filling with NULL if no match)?
questions.explanation: A LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table regardless of whether there is a matching row in the right table.

title: HTTP, REST APIs & Backend Services
plainExplanation: Web communication relies on HTTP protocols. Clients (browsers, mobile apps) send HTTP requests (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) with headers and JSON payloads to server endpoints. The server processes business logic, talks to the database, and sends back HTTP status codes and responses.
whyItMatters: Modern software systems are distributed. Mastering APIs enables you to build full-stack web applications, microservices, and mobile app backends.
learningObjectives: Understand HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) and status codes (200, 201, 400, 401, 404, 500)
Build RESTful endpoints returning structured JSON responses
Implement authentication tokens and request validation
commonMistakes: Using GET requests for operations that mutate database state
Returning status 200 OK when an internal server exception occurred

questions.prompt: Which HTTP status code indicates a resource was successfully created on the server?
questions.explanation: 201 Created is the standard HTTP status code for successful resource creation via POST/PUT.
